conversation.content:
Hello there. I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood by checking in on how you’re feeling emotionally.  

Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s a quick, well-studied set of 10 questions that screens for symptoms of depression and anxiety that can show up after childbirth. Anything you share stays between us unless safety requires otherwise, and there’s no “right” answer—only what’s true for you.  

We’ll go through the questions one by one, focusing on how you’ve felt over the past seven days. Each question will take just a moment, and you can answer in your own words. Ready to start?

First, thinking about the past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has laughter felt hard to come by?

Honestly, I can’t remember the last time I really laughed. Most days it feels like even smiling takes effort. I’ll see something on my phone that used to make me giggle, and it’s like I can’t get there—just sort of… flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No… not really. I might force a little chuckle if someone else is laughing, but it feels fake. Nothing seems truly funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now it all feels like one more chore. I still go through the motions, but inside I’m just… blah. Even thinking about the weekend doesn’t spark anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah, all the time. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a terrible mom.” Yesterday he spit up a lot after feeding and I sat there crying, convinced it was because I hadn’t burped him right. My partner keeps saying these things just happen, but I can’t shake the feeling that it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. My heart races out of nowhere, and I keep playing out awful scenes in my head—like the baby stopping breathing in his sleep or me dropping him. Nothing specific triggers it; the worries just show up and latch on. I’ll tell myself it’s unlikely, but the anxious feeling lingers for a while before it eases off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, that happens too. I’ll be sitting on the couch, everything looks calm, and suddenly my chest gets tight, my thoughts start racing, and I feel like something awful is about to happen. It’s like an alarm going off inside me for no real reason. I have to remind myself to breathe slowly until the feeling passes—usually after a few minutes—but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding, laundry’s everywhere, and I just freeze, thinking, “I can’t do all this.” I usually manage to push through the essentials, but it’s like walking through thick mud—every step feels heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. Even when the baby is finally down and the house is quiet, my mind keeps spinning with worries and this heavy, sad feeling. I’ll lie there for an hour or two, sometimes longer, staring at the ceiling. When I do nod off, I jerk awake at every little sound, heart pounding, and then it’s hard to drift back. I’m exhausted, but sleep just won’t come easily.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be feeding the baby or just folding tiny onesies and feel this wave of sadness hit me out of nowhere. Sometimes tears come without warning, other times it’s just this ache in my chest that sits there. I keep waiting for it to pass, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… I’ve cried three times in the past week. Once was after a phone call when Grandma asked how I was doing and I just broke down. Another time the baby wouldn’t settle and I felt so useless I sat on the nursery floor sobbing. It’s like the tears are right under the surface all the time.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never felt like I wanted to be gone or to harm myself. I just want to feel better for my baby’s sake and mine.

You've shared that, most days, laughter and excitement feel out of reach and even simple tasks feel like walking through mud. Waves of worry, tight-chested panic, and a constant gray sadness have become familiar, while sleep brings little relief. Despite these heavy feelings, you remain clear that you want to feel better for yourself and your baby, and you have not had thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete loss of ability to find things funny, only managing forced laughter</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure—activities once enjoyed now feel like chores and evoke no positive anticipation, matching "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, near-daily self-blame ("all the time") tied to routine infant behaviors, indicating the highest level of endorsed option "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports experiencing anxiety "pretty much every day" with physical symptoms (racing heart) and intrusive catastrophic thoughts, matching the "Yes, very often" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms and racing thoughts, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage routine tasks, and needing strenuous effort to complete essentials, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes most-of-the-time sleep disruption due to unhappiness: prolonged sleep-onset, repeated waking, and inability to return to sleep.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness that occurs "pretty much every day" with unexpected tears and persistent chest ache, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes triggered by everyday stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score ≥14 indicates probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>; at 26, your score is well above this threshold. You describe <sym>loss of interest</sym> and <sym>pleasure</sym> (<med>anhedonia</med>), <sym>daily sadness</sym>, <sym>tearfulness</sym>, <sym>excessive self-blame</sym>, <sym>early-morning wakening</sym> with racing thoughts, and <sym>panic-like episodes</sym> that meet screening criteria for a <med>Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset</med>. <quote>Nothing seems truly funny anymore</quote> and <quote>I'm drowning in small stuff</quote> underscore functional impairment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to review these results
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> and, if appropriate, <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Enlist practical help-partner, family, or postpartum doula-for night feeds and household tasks so you can get 4-6 hours of uninterrupted rest
4. Practice 5-minute breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic symptoms</sym> spike; schedule them before typical daily triggers
5. Limit doom-scrolling; replace late-night phone use with a dim-light audiobook or relaxation app to ease into sleep
6. Plan brief, low-pressure outings (10-minute stroller walk, porch coffee with a friend) to reintroduce manageable enjoyment
7. Keep the 24-hr <med>Postpartum Support International</med> helpline 1-800-944-4773 in your phone for immediate peer support
8. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (baby approx. weeks–months old)  
Date: [today]  

I. Symptoms / Concerns endorsed  
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
- Daily low mood, tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re parenting (Q3)  
- Persistent, unprovoked anxiety, panic spells (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning” in routine tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance problems not explained solely by infant care (Q7)  
- No self-harm ideation (Q10)  

II. Pattern  
All symptoms present “most days” for ≥ 1 week; functional impairment evident (household tasks “heavy,” social withdrawal, prolonged bedtime latency).  

III. Screening significance  
EPDS equivalent score ≈ 21–23 (highly elevated range); meets screening threshold for probable major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety symptoms.  

IV. Risk factors identified  
- Persistent sadness, loss of pleasure, crying spells  
- Sleep disruption tied to rumination/worry  
- Intense guilt / worthlessness regarding infant care  
- Recurrent panic-like episodes  
- Absence of protective factor: no suicidal ideation reported  

V. Safety  
Denies active self-harm thoughts; no plan or intent. Continue to monitor given high symptom load.  

VI. Next steps (screening level)  
Recommend expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialist for comprehensive evaluation and discussion of evidence-based treatment options.
